Retrieval tools compound the harm through a stall failure mode that blocks 52 percent of runs. Headline-only summaries, reduced to one sentence plus metadata pointers, save 80 percent of Zone B's tokens but produce scores indistinguishable from verbose summaries. The tree's value proposition — summaries as a compression layer for sessions that exceed the window — remains untested because the overflow regime was economically impractical to reach on available providers.
reports/metrics/ds-star-search-ranking-report.md:5:Context-tree reorganizes an agent's linear conversation trace into a summary-headed tree so that a long-running session sees branch summaries instead of raw history, pulling detail back on demand through retrieval tools. A prior DS-STAR pass found that summary-based search ranks the correct branch at position 11–17 of 19 for most questions, directing the model to the wrong branch and causing a 52 percent stall rate. This pass fixed the ranking through two complementary mechanisms, tested offline on one frozen store with 12 paraphrased questions: fingerprint-enriched search documents — file paths, identifiers, and symbols extracted deterministically from raw events and appended to each branch's summary-based search document — move beam search alone from 2 of 12 to 7 of 12 questions with the correct branch in the top 3; adding rank-reciprocal fusion with grep on distinctive query terms reaches 10 of 12. The two remaining failures are questions whose query text contains no distinctive identifiers: one abstract concept query and one with only short generic terms. Both mechanisms are landed in the codebase with 580 passing tests. No live model run has been conducted; the next step is a live verification at W=32,768 to measure whether the improved ranking reduces the stall rate.
reports/metrics/ds-star-multi-index-report.md:5:Context-tree reorganizes an agent's linear conversation trace into a summary-headed tree, so a long-running session sees branch summaries instead of raw history and pulls detail back on demand through retrieval tools. A prior pass had improved search ranking from 2 of 12 to 10 of 12 questions with the correct branch in the top three, yet live scores did not move; this pass asked why. Three findings, each measured. First, the tree had never been tested in the regime it exists for: the question set's "head" stratum was cut against the smallest window's truncation boundary, which does not place answers outside a wider window's raw tail. A rebuilt set puts every answer provably out of reach. Second, an oracle probe that hands the model the correct branch on the first call recovers most but not all of the gap, and how much depends entirely on which question set it is measured against: on the set where a real-search baseline also exists, the oracle recovers 19 of the 21 points that baseline loses, leaving about 8% of the loss after retrieval; on a harder set built later it reaches only 13 of 25 against a ground truth of 25 of 25, but no real-search baseline was ever run there, so that gap cannot be split between ranking and extraction. Third, the post-retrieval residual is payload density: a phase replay is 26 KB with the answer on one of its 384 lines, while a command-facet entry averages 24 tokens, so a mediocre rank over cheap entries costs a few hundred tokens where a perfect rank over expensive ones still buries the answer. Multiple indexes raise coverage from 5–6 of 17 questions to 9, but only when a query is routed to one index; fusing indexes by relevance drops it to 6. The main limitation is that all of it rests on one 754-event session and 17 questions, and that six of those questions cannot be served by any single-entry index at all.

reports/metrics/loop8-interim.md:11:An agent's prompt normally contains the transcript of everything it has done, so the prompt grows with the length of the task and eventually exceeds the context window of the model. Context-tree is a context-management layer built to remove that limit: it writes the full history to disk, segments it into phases of work, and assembles the prompt from a bounded working set — one headline line per completed phase, the full detail of the phase in progress, and tools with which the agent can retrieve anything older on demand. Two parts of that working set could still grow without limit: the headline list gains a line per phase, and several metadata lists accumulate across phases. This report describes two changes that cap both (the prompt lists only the 40 most recent phases individually, folding everything older into a single line that says what was removed and how to get it back; no rendered list may exceed 40 entries) and measures the result against the ordinary transcript. On a synthetic 200-phase task the tree prompt is constant at 9,062 tokens from phase 80 onward, while the transcript grows by about 284 tokens per phase and exceeds a 16k context window at phase 56 and a 32k window at phase 113; a live API call per arm at phase 200 confirmed this — the transcript was rejected by the model, the tree prompt was answered. The same evaluation exposed and fixed a caching defect that had been re-writing the same ~33k-token prefix to the provider's cache five times per run. Tokens, turns, and graded accuracy are the primary metrics throughout; dollar figures appear only as derived values at one model's prices. Finally, we tested retrieval of folded material live: asked at phase 200 to recall a decision from phase 10 — whose description appears nowhere in the prompt — without using its vocabulary, the model searched for and recovered all three planted facts in 15 of 15 replicates.

> **TENTATIVE. Nothing here is shipped — this is all in development.** It reorganizes the loop
> (Tier 1) into a three-stage pipeline and folds in the 2026-09-09 offline findings. The current
> code still runs the Zone A/B/C loop below, but that loop is being *replaced*, not defended — it is
> not an authoritative baseline. Evidence tags: `[BUILT]` = code exists in `packages/`;
> `[OFFLINE]` = validated on a proxy only; `[DESIGN]` = designed, not built. **Nothing here is
> live-validated** — promote a stage only when a live run clears it.

Two scorers feed one decider; retrieval serves on demand. The classifier scores query-independent
state (has the topic shifted); the retriever scores query-dependent relevance (what matches this
turn); the assembler-ejector decides what to keep, cache-stable, to a soft target.

A prior DS-STAR pass found that summary-based search ranks the correct branch at position 11–17 of 19 for most questions, directing the model to the wrong branch and causing a 52 percent stall rate. First, the tree had never been tested in the regime it exists for: the question set's "head" stratum was cut against the smallest window's truncation boundary, which does not place answers outside a wider window's raw tail. Second, an oracle probe that hands the model the correct branch on the first call recovers most but not all of the gap, and how much depends entirely on which question set it is measured against: on the set where a real-search baseline also exists, the oracle recovers 19 of the 21 points that baseline loses, leaving about 8% of the loss after retrieval; on a harder set built later it reaches only 13 of 25 against a ground truth of 25 of 25, but no real-search baseline was ever run there, so that gap cannot be split between ranking and extraction. Third, the post-retrieval residual is payload density: a phase replay is 26 KB with the answer on one of its 384 lines, while a command-facet entry averages 24 tokens, so a mediocre rank over cheap entries costs a few hundred tokens where a perfect rank over expensive ones still buries the answer. reports/metrics/loop8-interim.md:11:An agent's prompt normally contains the transcript of everything it has done, so the prompt grows with the length of the task and eventually exceeds the context window of the model. Context-tree is a context-management layer built to remove that limit: it writes the full history to disk, segments it into phases of work, and assembles the prompt from a bounded working set — one headline line per completed phase, the full detail of the phase in progress, and tools with which the agent can retrieve anything older on demand. Two parts of that working set could still grow without limit: the headline list gains a line per phase, and several metadata lists accumulate across phases. This report describes two changes that cap both (the prompt lists only the 40 most recent phases individually, folding everything older into a single line that says what was removed and how to get it back; no rendered list may exceed 40 entries) and measures the result against the ordinary transcript. On a synthetic 200-phase task the tree prompt is constant at 9,062 tokens from phase 80 onward, while the transcript grows by about 284 tokens per phase and exceeds a 16k context window at phase 56 and a 32k window at phase 113; a live API call per arm at phase 200 confirmed this — the transcript was rejected by the model, the tree prompt was answered. The same evaluation exposed and fixed a caching defect that had been re-writing the same ~33k-token prefix to the provider's cache five times per run. Tokens, turns, and graded accuracy are the primary metrics throughout; dollar figures appear only as derived values at one model's prices. Finally, we tested retrieval of folded material live: asked at phase 200 to recall a decision from phase 10 — whose description appears nowhere in the prompt — without using its vocabulary, the model searched for and recovered all three planted facts in 15 of 15 replicates.

That reframe (paper, not product) plus "nothing is shipped" clarifies everything — and the search just gave me a real, evidence-based answer to your retrieval-order question. Let me give it straight.

## What our results actually show about retrieval order

**The on-demand-vs-retrieve-first *order* was never A/B-tested.** But the repo carries strong *adjacent* evidence, and it's more interesting than "we don't know":

- **Below the overflow regime (every window prior work could afford to test): on-demand-from-summaries LOSES.** The DS-STAR passes are blunt about it — the tree arm scored **≈0 vs truncate-tail** because (a) summary-based search **ranks the wrong branch** (11–17 of 19), and (b) retrieval tool overhead **burns 15–20K tokens** that the tail spends on raw answer-bearing content (`ds-star-live-verification`, `ds-star-retrieval-pass`, `ds-star-tree-tail-iter1`).
- **In the overflow regime (session ≫ window): the tree WINS** — bounded prompt (constant 9,062 tokens while the transcript blows past the window), and at phase 200 it **recovered a phase-10 fact 15/15** live while the raw transcript was outright rejected (`context-growth`, `loop8-interim`).
- **The catch:** that overflow regime was *"economically impractical to reach"* on prior providers, so **the entire value claim is barely tested live.**

So "retrieve on demand, last" isn't an established result — it's a design that **only pays off in overflow**, and overflow is exactly what nobody could afford to test. That's the honest state.

## How we establish it — and why *now*

**The 8.2K model is the unlock.** It makes the overflow regime *trivially cheap* to reach — the thing every DS-STAR pass said it couldn't afford. So the way to settle the retrieval order (and the tree's core thesis) is the **overflow-regime A/B**, which is what the agent-loop escalation *becomes*:

> On a real overflowing session under the 8.2K window: **truncate-tail** vs **tree (summaries + on-demand retrieval)** vs **reducer-router**, measured on task success + tokens. Below overflow, expect truncate-tail to win (prior evidence); the question is whether the tree/on-demand wins *in overflow* — where truncate-tail literally can't fit.

That's not a side quest — for a **paper**, it's arguably the **headline experiment**: *the tree's value proposition, tested in the regime it exists for, which prior work never reached.*

## The doc, given "it's a paper and nothing is shipped"

You're right — I'll stop treating the Tier-1 Zone A/B/C loop as "current code to preserve." There's no product; `algorithm.md` should be **one clean statement of current best understanding**, with **rejected designs thrown out** and **only the evidence/learnings kept** (Zone B "measured inert" stays as a finding; "Zone A/B/C is what runs" goes). I can do that reconciliation pass.

**So two things, your call on order:**
1. **The overflow-regime experiment** (8.2K window, truncate-tail vs tree vs router) — the paper's central result, now finally affordable.
2. **The algorithm.md cleanup** — collapse it to current-best-understanding, drop the shipped/product framing.

Which first? My vote: **the overflow experiment** — it's the missing keystone the whole programme has been unable to reach, and the paper needs it.

**Now we're finding the breaks — two distinct ones, which is exactly the point.** With docs big enough to actually pressure the 8.2K window:

| arm | outcome | detail |
|---|---|---|
| truncate-tail (raw + recency) | **CRASH** | HTTP 500 — the weak model emitted **malformed tool-call JSON** once raw reads filled context near the window (peak 5641) |
| full-pipeline (router + priority) | **read-loop** | 40 reads / 9 re-reads / maxTurns; **no crash, no overflow** (reducer kept peak at 5972) but the agent never committed to `write_file` |

**What this tells us — the pieces work; the weak model is the bottleneck:**
- **The middleware did its job:** the router reducer kept reads small, so the full pipeline **never overflowed and never crashed** — whereas raw truncate-tail pushed the context large enough that the **weak 8.2K model degraded into invalid tool-call JSON**. So footprint control *prevented* the failure the baseline hit.
- **But the full pipeline still failed the task** — via the **restricted-tool read-loop** we saw earlier: with only `read_file`/`write_file`, the weak model reads endlessly and won't commit to writing. That's a **model-behavior break, not a middleware-logic break** — the reducer/eviction can't force a weak model to finish.

To disentangle "weak model vs middleware," the clean test is the **same pipeline on a stronger model** (the 27B, artificially windowed). Let me launch that in the background while I write this up.
